title: Transport
summary: How capillaries, arteries and veins are adapted for blood transport, what happens when coronary arteries are blocked, and how water is pulled up xylem in plants. HL adds tissue fluid and lymph, double circulation, the heart and cardiac cycle, root pressure and phloem translocation.

keyterms.definition: Narrow, highly branched vessel with a wall one cell thick, sometimes with fenestrations (pores), adapted for exchange with tissues.
Vessel carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure; thick wall of smooth muscle and elastic fibres, narrow lumen.
Vessel returning blood to the heart at low pressure; thin wall, wide lumen and valves to prevent backflow.
Layers of artery and vein walls: tunica intima (endothelium), tunica media (smooth muscle, elastic fibres) and tunica externa (collagen).
Build-up of fatty deposits (plaque) in artery walls, narrowing the lumen and increasing the risk of clot formation.
Blockage of a coronary artery, often by a clot at a plaque, cutting oxygen supply to heart muscle and causing coronary heart disease or heart attack.
Transpiration from leaves creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water, held by cohesion, up the xylem; adhesion to walls also helps.
Continuous tube of dead cells with lignified walls, no contents or end walls, and pits; carries water and minerals from roots to leaves.
Fluid forced out of capillaries by pressure filtration at the arterial end that bathes cells; most is reabsorbed at the venous end.
Excess tissue fluid drained into lymphatic vessels, which have valves and thin walls, and returned to the blood near the heart.
Circulation in which blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: pulmonary circuit to the lungs and systemic circuit to the body.
Pacemaker: specialized cardiac muscle cells in the right atrium wall that initiate each heartbeat.
Sequence of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole) of atria and ventricles, with valves opening and closing due to pressure changes.
Positive pressure in xylem generated by active transport of mineral ions into root xylem, drawing in water by osmosis; important when transpiration is low.
Phloem sieve tubes have sieve plates and little cytoplasm; companion cells beside them have many mitochondria and actively load sucrose.
Movement of phloem sap, mainly sucrose, from sources to sinks, driven by hydrostatic pressure differences.

questions.prompt: Which feature of capillaries most directly adapts them for exchange of materials with tissues?
options: Walls only one cell thick, some with fenestrations
A thick layer of smooth muscle
Valves to prevent backflow
A wide lumen to carry blood at high pressure
questions.explanation: Thin walls with pores minimize diffusion distance and allow some leakage of fluid. Branching into huge networks also gives a large surface area.

questions.statement: Arteries have thick walls containing smooth muscle and elastic fibres to withstand and maintain high blood pressure.
questions.explanation: Blood leaves the ventricles at high pressure; thick, elastic, muscular walls resist bursting and help keep pressure high between beats.

questions.text: Veins contain ___ that prevent backflow of low-pressure blood.
questions.explanation: Blood pressure in veins is low, so pocket valves close if blood begins to flow backward, keeping flow towards the heart.

questions.prompt: Match each structure to its description.
questions.explanation: Arteries and veins share the three tunica layers, but arteries have a much thicker tunica media. Capillaries are just endothelium, sometimes fenestrated.

questions.prompt: What is the role of elastic fibres in the walls of arteries?
options: They pump blood like a second heart
They prevent the blood from clotting
They stretch when the ventricles pump and recoil between beats, helping maintain pressure
They allow nutrients to leave the artery
questions.explanation: Elastic recoil pushes blood onward during diastole, smoothing flow and keeping pressure high. Arteries do not pump; muscle in the tunica media adjusts the diameter.

questions.statement: Veins have a narrower lumen than arteries of similar size.
questions.explanation: Veins have a wider lumen and thinner walls, which offers less resistance to the slow, low-pressure flow of blood back to the heart.

questions.prompt: How does contraction of skeletal muscles help return blood to the heart in veins?
options: It increases the heart rate directly
It actively transports blood through the vein wall
It forces the valves open in both directions
It squeezes adjacent veins, and valves ensure the blood moves towards the heart
questions.explanation: Veins often run between muscles; when muscles contract they compress the thin-walled veins, and the valves only allow flow in one direction.

questions.prompt: Put the events leading to a heart attack in order.
items: Endothelium of a coronary artery is damaged
Fatty plaque builds up in the artery wall
The lumen narrows, reducing blood flow
A blood clot forms and blocks the artery
Heart muscle beyond the blockage is deprived of oxygen and dies
questions.explanation: Atherosclerosis narrows coronary arteries; occlusion by a clot cuts off oxygen to part of the heart muscle, which can no longer respire aerobically.

questions.text: Pulse rate is often measured by pressing two fingers on the ___ artery in the wrist.
questions.explanation: Each surge of blood from the left ventricle stretches arteries, which can be felt where an artery lies near the surface, e.g. the radial artery in the wrist or the carotid in the neck.

questions.prompt: Which factor is associated with an increased risk of coronary heart disease?
options: Regular aerobic exercise
Smoking
A diet low in saturated fat
Low blood pressure
questions.explanation: Smoking damages the endothelium and raises blood pressure, promoting atherosclerosis. Epidemiological studies show correlation; experiments help establish causation.

questions.prompt: What provides the main force that moves water up the xylem during transpiration?
options: Active transport by xylem cells
Contraction of the xylem walls
Root cells pumping water upward
Tension created by evaporation of water from leaf cell walls
questions.explanation: Water evaporating from mesophyll cell walls is replaced by water pulled from the xylem, creating tension that draws the whole column upward.

questions.text: Water molecules attract each other by hydrogen bonding, a property called ___, so the water column in the xylem is not broken.
questions.explanation: Cohesion lets tension be transmitted down the column from leaves to roots. Adhesion is attraction between water and other substances such as the xylem walls.

questions.statement: Xylem vessels are living cells with cytoplasm that pump water upward.
questions.explanation: Mature xylem vessels are dead and empty. Water moves passively, pulled by tension; no ATP is used by the vessels.

questions.prompt: Match each feature of xylem vessels to its function.

pairs.right: Continuous tube from root to leaf
Let water move sideways between vessels

questions.explanation: Xylem is a dead, hollow, reinforced pipeline adapted to carry water under tension.

questions.prompt: What is adhesion in the context of water transport in xylem?
options: Attraction between water molecules and the hydrophilic walls of the xylem
Attraction between water molecules
Movement of water into roots by osmosis
Binding of minerals to water
questions.explanation: Adhesion to cellulose and lignin in vessel walls helps water rise by capillary action and stops the column pulling away from the walls.

questions.statement: Transport of water through xylem during transpiration does not require the plant to use ATP.
questions.explanation: The energy comes from evaporation (ultimately heat from the sun); the plant spends no metabolic energy pulling water up.

questions.prompt: Put the stages in the path of water through a plant in order.
items: Mesophyll cell walls in the leaf
Evaporation and diffusion out through stomata
questions.explanation: Water enters root hairs by osmosis, crosses the cortex to the xylem, rises to the leaves and evaporates into air spaces before diffusing out of stomata.

questions.prompt: How are vascular tissues arranged in a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem?
options: A single central core of xylem surrounded by phloem
Scattered randomly through the stem
Vascular bundles in a ring, with xylem towards the centre and phloem towards the outside
Phloem towards the centre and xylem towards the outside
questions.explanation: Dicot stems have a ring of vascular bundles near the outside, each with phloem outermost, then cambium, then xylem facing the pith.

questions.prompt: Where is the xylem located in a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root?
options: In a ring of bundles near the epidermis
In the centre of the root, often in a star or X shape, with phloem between its arms
Only in the root hairs
In the outer cortex
questions.explanation: Roots have a central vascular cylinder: xylem forms the core with phloem in the gaps, surrounded by the endodermis and cortex.

questions.text: Evaporation of water from leaves creates ___ (negative pressure) in the xylem, which pulls water upward.
questions.explanation: Under tension the xylem sap is pulled rather than pushed; lignified walls stop the vessels collapsing inward.

lessons.title: Tissue fluid, the heart and phloem

questions.prompt: How is tissue fluid formed and reabsorbed in capillary beds?
options: It is actively secreted by capillary cells and absorbed by lymph only
It is forced out at the venous end and reabsorbed at the arterial end
High pressure at the arterial end forces fluid out (pressure filtration); at the venous end, lower pressure lets most return
It diffuses out evenly along the whole capillary and none returns
questions.explanation: Pressure falls along the capillary. At the arterial end pressure exceeds the osmotic pull of plasma proteins, so fluid leaves; at the venous end the balance reverses and most fluid re-enters.

questions.statement: Tissue fluid contains large plasma proteins, which are forced out of capillaries along with the fluid.
questions.explanation: Plasma proteins are too large to pass through capillary walls, so they stay in the blood and help draw water back in at the venous end.

questions.text: Excess tissue fluid drains into ___ vessels and is returned to the blood near the heart.
questions.explanation: Lymph ducts have thin walls with gaps for fluid to enter and valves for one-way flow; lymph rejoins the blood in veins near the heart.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its description.

pairs.right: Blood passes through the heart once per circuit
Prevent backflow from ventricles to atria
Prevent backflow from arteries to ventricles

questions.explanation: Mammals have a double circulation and a four-chambered heart whose valves ensure one-way flow; the SA node sets the rhythm.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of a double circulation compared with the single circulation of fish?
options: Blood returning from the lungs is re-pressurized by the heart, so it reaches body tissues at high pressure
Blood passes through the gills twice for more oxygen
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are mixed
The heart needs fewer chambers
questions.explanation: In fish, blood loses pressure in the gill capillaries before going to the body. In mammals it returns to the heart after the lungs and is pumped again, delivering it quickly to tissues.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of the cardiac cycle in order, starting with atrial systole.
items: Atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles
Ventricles contract and the atrioventricular valves close
Ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure and the semilunar valves open
Ventricles relax and the semilunar valves close
Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, AV valves open and ventricles fill
questions.explanation: Valves open and close passively in response to pressure differences, so blood always flows from atria to ventricles to arteries.

questions.prompt: Why is the wall of the left ventricle thicker than that of the right ventricle?
options: It receives more blood from the lungs
It contains the SA node
It must contract for longer
It pumps blood through the whole systemic circulation, which requires a higher pressure
questions.explanation: Both ventricles pump the same volume, but the left must generate enough pressure to push blood around the body; the right only pumps to the nearby lungs, whose delicate capillaries need lower pressure.

questions.statement: The sinoatrial node is a group of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium that acts as the pacemaker.
questions.explanation: The SA node fires spontaneously; its signals spread through the atria and on to the ventricles, initiating each heartbeat.

questions.prompt: How is root pressure generated?
options: By tension created by evaporation from leaves
By active transport of mineral ions into the root xylem, so water follows by osmosis
By companion cells loading sucrose
By contraction of lignified xylem walls
questions.explanation: Pumping ions into the xylem lowers its water potential; water enters by osmosis and builds positive pressure. This is important when transpiration is low, e.g. before leaves open in spring.

questions.text: Phloem sieve tube elements are joined end to end by perforated ___ plates.
questions.explanation: Sieve plates let sap flow from one element to the next while keeping the tube's structure; xylem vessels, by contrast, lose their end walls completely.

questions.prompt: What is the role of companion cells in translocation?
options: They are dead cells that support the sieve tubes
They pull water up by transpiration
They have many mitochondria and actively load sucrose into the sieve tubes
They store starch for the sieve tubes
questions.explanation: Sieve tubes have very little cytoplasm and no nucleus, so companion cells carry out their metabolism, including the ATP-requiring loading of sucrose at sources.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of translocation in phloem in order.
items: Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at a source
Water enters the sieve tube by osmosis, raising hydrostatic pressure
Sap flows along the sieve tube towards lower pressure
Sucrose is unloaded at a sink and water leaves
questions.explanation: Loading at the source and unloading at the sink create a pressure difference that drives mass flow of sap from source to sink.
